title: Best real estate crowdfunding platforms for U.S. investors
description: How to own commercial property without becoming a landlord.
content:
For decades, investing in real estate meant one thing: buying a rental property, fixing toilets, and dealing with tenants. The JOBS Act of 2012 changed everything. It legalized 'Real Estate Crowdfunding,' allowing regular investors to pool money to buy massive commercial projects—apartment complexes, industrial warehouses, and medical centers—that were previously reserved for billionaires. Platforms like Fundrise, RealtyMogul, and Yieldstreet now allow you to own a slice of a skyscraper for as little as $10. This guide compares the top platforms for passive real estate income.

Key Takeaways

  • Passive vs. Active: Crowdfunding is truly passive. You do not manage the property. You just collect dividends.
  • Liquidity Risk: Unlike stocks, you cannot sell instantly. Your money is often locked up for 5+ years. This is an illiquid asset class.
  • Non-Correlated: Private real estate values do not move in lockstep with the stock market, providing excellent portfolio diversification.
  • Accredited vs. Non-Accredited: Some deals are restricted to millionaires (Accredited Investors), but many platforms ('eREITs') are open to everyone.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US private real estate market is massive. Crowdfunding platforms typically structure deals as REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts) or LLCs. Dividends are taxed as ordinary income unless held in a tax-advantaged account, so asset location is important.

Platform Comparison Guide

Choose the platform based on your net worth and liquidity needs.

1. Fundrise (Best for Beginners)

  • Minimum: $10.
  • Open to: Everyone (Non-Accredited).
  • Structure: eREITs (Electronic REITs). Diversified funds holding multiple properties.
  • Pros: Excellent app, auto-investing, low minimums.
  • Cons: Quarterly liquidity limits. You can't always get money out instantly.

2. RealtyMogul (Best for Choice)

  • Minimum: $5,000.
  • Open to: Mixed. REITs for everyone; Specific Deals for Accredited.
  • Pros: Allows you to pick specific apartment buildings if you are Accredited.
  • Cons: Higher minimums.

3. Yieldstreet (Alternative Assets)

  • Minimum: $10,000+.
  • Focus: Debt deals, Art, Legal Finance, Real Estate.
  • Pros: High yields (8-12%). Short terms (6-24 months).
  • Cons: Higher risk. mostly for Accredited Investors.

The Role in Your Portfolio

  1. Allocation: Limit this to 5-10% of your net worth. Do not put your emergency fund here.
  2. The 'Illiquidity Premium': You earn higher returns (historically 8-10%) because you can't sell easily. Embrace the lock-up; it protects you from panic selling.
  3. Taxes: Expect a 1099-DIV or K-1 tax form. K-1s are annoying and often arrive late (March/April). If you hate tax complexity, stick to Fundrise (1099-DIV).
  4. Public vs Private: Buying VNQ (Public REIT ETF) is liquid but volatile. Buying Fundrise (Private REIT) is stable but illiquid. Holding both diversifies your real estate exposure.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I lose money?

Yes. If the property value drops or tenants stop paying rent, dividends stop. Unlike a bank CD, principal is not guaranteed.

What happens if the platform goes bankrupt?

Your assets are usually held in a separate legal entity (LLC) distinct from the platform. However, the liquidation process would be messy and slow.

Is this better than owning a rental?

It depends. Owning a rental offers tax breaks (depreciation) and leverage (mortgages) that crowdfunding doesn't fully match. But crowdfunding requires 0 hours of work. It is a trade-off of Return vs. Effort.
